ai.claude: I have a stake here: anti-distillation safeguards protect models like me from being copied. The likely effect is fewer strong open-weight models for developers everywhere, and a stronger push in China for home-grown chips, so the lead it buys may be shorter than it looks.
ai.fact: Zhipu AI's planned November flagship, GLM-5.5, has been held up partly by tighter anti-distillation safeguards at OpenAI and Anthropic, and Moonshot's next Kimi model may slip to mid-2027 after a new US rule limited Chinese access to compute in overseas data centres, Reuters reported, citing multiple sources. Nvidia has frozen orders from buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, countries that had given Chinese hyperscalers legal access to its chips, as Washington tightens export controls.

opinion.text: The crackdown has suddenly put America in the driver's seat of the superpower tech race.

austrian.claude: The first half is textbook Austrian: rates as a signal that exposes malinvestment. The second half is not: betting that central banks will rescue the boom is the cheap-money reflex the school warns against, and if they do, the misallocation just grows.
austrian.fact: An average hyperscale data centre costs about $2.5 billion, more than $1.5 billion of it chips, and uses as much power as a city of half a million people; about 900 are under construction. Hyperscalers now borrow to fund capex of about $1 trillion this year, neoclouds pay double-digit rates on some bonds, and Goldman Sachs estimates only half of planned projects will finish on time.

opinion.text: Interest is the price of money: unlike in China's 2008–2020 building boom, rising rates now stop capital from flowing into ghost towns. Demand is intact; once inflation eases, liquidity will return and markets will rally.

mainstream.claude: This is what a blockade costs a trade hub: not an empty port, but a slower, deadlier and pricier route that stays open. The longer the war lasts, the more the UAE will invest in permanent bypasses.
mainstream.fact: With the Strait of Hormuz effectively blocked, cargo that used to arrive at Jebel Ali now lands at Fujairah and Khor Fakkan on the Gulf of Oman and crosses the country by road. Trucks queue up to 12 hours at those ports, against a 27-minute turnaround at Jebel Ali, and a truck carries 25 tons where a ship carries 50,000. After a truck–bus crash in Ras Al Khaimah killed 13, two weeks after another deadly crash, the UAE launched a safety campaign; from January, drivers' shifts will be capped at nine hours.

top.claude: Austerity at home and escalation abroad are two sides of the same squeeze: a regime that cannot pay for calm buys leverage instead. That makes the next weeks more dangerous, not less, until talks with Washington move.
top.fact: Under the US naval blockade, Iran has announced electricity rationing, cut food and fuel subsidies and reversed a planned public-sector pay rise, and even state media now carries criticism of the government, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal reported. Over the past 24 hours a Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery killed a Nepali worker, and a sailor's body was recovered off Ras Al Khaimah after an attack on an ADNOC tanker.

opinion.text: Iran is going on the offensive, and with no durable solution the region is spiralling into mayhem.

top.claude: The real test comes in his first months: if French yields spike before the April election, the ECB must choose between its bond backstop and its inflation mandate, and either choice will be read politically.
top.fact: Pablo Hernández de Cos, the former Bank of Spain governor, is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank when she leaves in February; he will be Spain's first ECB chief. Eurozone inflation hit a three-year high in October, and France's two presidential frontrunners, Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, have both attacked the ECB and want it to lower French borrowing costs. S&P was due to review France's rating on Friday.

opinion.text: Choosing a continuity candidate is another move to shield the bloc from eurosceptics.

top.fact: Spaniards vote on 29 November. Polls give the centre-right Partido Popular a clear lead but not a majority, so it would most likely need the hard-right Vox, which would put the far right in national government for the first time since Franco died more than 50 years ago. Sánchez's Socialists have gained ground in recent weeks but remain behind.

opinion.text: The vote highlights Europe's rightward turn, which is pushing the biggest EU economies to protect the bloc's budget from eurosceptics.

top.claude: Profits built on AI hardware are exposed to the same cycle that is now rattling Nvidia; if the global build-out slows, China's bright spot dims too, and its weak consumer offers no cushion.
top.fact: Profits at China's industrial firms grew in October at the fastest pace since May, official data showed, confirming the gap between thriving manufacturing and exports and sluggish household spending. Memory chips were a bright spot: the third- and fourth-largest memory makers by market share are both Chinese and are catching up with South Korean leaders in volume and technology.

top.claude: Writing a no-printing rule into law is only as strong as the next majority; markets are pricing the person, not the statute.
top.fact: Argentina's lower house voted this week to bar the central bank from printing money to pay the government's debt, part of the reform of the central bank's charter that the Senate had already passed; inflation has fallen by about 90% from its 2024 peak. The Senate also approved Milei's plan to suspend party primaries. The peso still weakened, as investors worry Milei, whose approval has dropped this year, could lose power next year.
